paper_title: Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in persistent task state, yet repeatedly process interaction histories describing how that progress was achieved. This raises a natural question: can long-horizon context instead be organized around reusable progress rather than the history that produced it? In this paper, we introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects. Rather than treating compressed histories or reconstructed accounts of progress as the primary basis for continuation, CarryOn builds a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions. A core challenge is keeping this reusable basis valid after its surrounding history is retired: how can CarryOn update the basis without reconstructing the full representation at every fold? CarryOn maintains carrier records across folds, revising affected records against bound evidence and applicable environment checks while carrying forward unaffected records and jointly updating execution context. Experiments on OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus show improved gains of 5.8% and 7.0% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in two places: persistent task state, which embodies what has been achieved, and interaction history, which records how it was achieved (Yi et al., 2026). As shown in Figure 1, once images have been inserted into presentation or measurements have been entered into report, the resulting task state already captures that progress for later steps to inspect and modify (Yang et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026). As execution continues, this redundancy grows: agents repeatedly process accounts of how results already available in the task state were produced. Existing methods manage growing histories by summarizing, retrieving, or pruning past interactions (Wu et al., 2026b; Packer et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Kang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025), or by translating them into explicit progress records and structured task states (Wu et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2024). These approaches reduce context growth, but when they substitute for reusable task results, they make continuation depend on redundant, selective account that can drift from the state the agent directly inspects and modifies. We challenge this reliance on reconstructed accounts of progress with an object-oriented view of long-horizon context, in which reusable task objects form the basis for continuation. These objects include work products, source-grounded findings, and application states that remain usable under explicit conditions. The agent can recover relevant information through direct inspection and use of these objects, while context supplies the complementary information needed to continue. To realize this view, we introduce CarryOn, context runtime that organizes the agents context into three complementary components: continuation carriers, which bind reusable content or object references to their conditions of use; execution context, which preserves active goals, applicable constraints, and unresolved issues not captured by the carriers; and live tail, which retains interactions since the most recent successful fold. Top: In slide-editing task, the working presentation and exported images carry completed editing progress, while remaining constraints and save verification stay explicit, reducing active context from 42.4K to 14.4K tokens (66.0%). Bottom: In lab-report task, the working document carries completed edits, while unresolved calculations remain explicit, reducing active context from 58.4K to 23.5K tokens (59.7%). central challenge in building object-oriented long-horizon context is retiring interaction history once progress becomes reusable without losing the information required for continuation, which poses three challenges: 1) how to identify reusable progress beyond its surrounding history: Some results still depend on prior interactions for interpretation or use. CarryOn captures these dependencies as conditions of use explicit in continuation carriers. 2) how to maintain reusable progress as the task evolves: Retaining record does not by itself establish that its content remains supported or its referenced state remains available. CarryOn binds updates to supporting sources and applicable environment checks; across folds, affected records are revised while unaffected records are carried forward. Finally, what must remain explicit when the corresponding history is retired: Task objects do not need to capture the goals, constraints, and unresolved issues that guide subsequent execution. CarryOn jointly updates continuation carriers and execution context to preserve this complementary information, while keeping recent interactions in live tail. Once validated, these updates are committed through fold, replacing the covered interaction history with the resulting objectoriented context view. In this way, CarryOn progressively reorganizes the long-horizon context around reusable task objects while preserving the information required for the agent to continue. In our experiments, object-oriented context management improves task performance while substantially reducing context cost. Our method, CarryOn, lifts Claude Opus 4.7 from 43.9% to 49.7% (+5.8%) on OSWorld 2.0 for long-horizon computer use and from 49% to 56% (+7%) on BrowseComp-Plus for long-horizon browsing. At the same time, it reduces total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, and total cost by 35.9% and 7.1%, on the two benchmarks, respectively. Compressing history alone is insufficient for continued execution: organizing context around reusable progress improves over generic compression, while the full CarryOn runtime further improves over the same principles implemented through repeated summarization. Continuation carriers and execution context play complementary roles, and reusable progress is typically maintained across folds rather than repeatedly reconstructed.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Context Compression and Selection. Existing methods reduce long-horizon context by compressing, pruning, summarizing, or selectively retrieving prior interactions (Wei et al., 2026). Compression and pruning range from prompt-level compression (Jiang et al., 2023; 2024) to removal of redundant or outdated interactions (Xiao et al., 2026). Summarization methods periodically replace accumulated interactions with compact reasoning states or learned summaries (Wu et al., 2026b; Kang et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025), while branch-based execution can return only compact subtask results (Sun et al., 2025). External-history methods instead keep the active context bounded while preserving access to earlier interactions outside the prompt (Packer et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026), and some systems validate compressed representations against subsequent execution to reduce information loss (Chen et al., 2026b). State Externalization and Context Reconstruction. Complementary approaches represent task progress explicitly, reducing reliance on raw interaction history alone. Some maintain an internal state by integrating prior memory with new observations (Zhou et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025), while others use structured representations, such as execution-state trees, persistent variables, or task records (Chen et al., 2026a; Tian et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026a; Ma et al., 2026). Recent systems further externalize state into persistent workspaces and reconstruct the models working context through snapshots or programmatic selection (Yu et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026). Across these approaches, continuation is primarily organized around compressed interaction history or externally maintained state. Our approach instead makes reusable task objects the primary unit of continuation.

sections.title: 3.1 FRAMEWORK
sections.content: Figure 2 illustrates CarryOn, which organizes long-horizon continuation around reusable task objects rather than the interactions that produced them. Reusable objects carry established progress for subsequent inspection and use, while explicit context retains complementary continuation information. Alongside the agents interaction loop, Tracker identifies candidate reusable progress, which is bound to supporting evidence and, when applicable, checked by Grounder. Compiler jointly updates continuation carriers and execution context. After validation, the update replaces the covered interaction history through fold, while subsequent interactions form new live tail.

sections.title: 3.2 CONTEXT VIEW
sections.content: We organize the agents active context into three complementary components: continuation carriers, which expose reusable task objects; execution context, which preserves continuation information not captured by those carriers; and live tail, which retains interactions accumulated since the latest fold. Continuation Carriers. Continuation carriers expose reusable progress to subsequent execution. Each carrier has stable identity and records the reusable content or its location, together with conditions for reuse. Revisions create successor versions under the same identity, while unaffected carriers retain their records. Depending on where the reusable progress resides, CarryOn supports three forms of carriers: External Objects: External objects are work products that exist independently in the environment and can be reopened or modified, such as code files, documents, and spreadsheets. Their carrier records reference the underlying objects and describe the progress they capture together with conditions for reuse. Information Products: Information products capture reusable findings obtained through interaction, such as synthesized information or troubleshooting conclusions. When not materialized as persistent objects, the carriers store the findings directly, with supporting sources and reuse conditions. 3 Figure 2: Overview of the CarryOn framework. CarryOn maintains an object-oriented context view comprising continuation carriers, execution context, and live tail. When invoked, it tracks reusable progress, binds supporting evidence, checks relevant environment conditions, and jointly compiles carrier and execution-context updates. successful fold commits validated updates and retires covered live-tail interactions from active context, while interaction log remains append-only. Situated State: Situated state captures progress available only within particular application, session, or workflow. Reusing such progress requires returning to the environment in which the state resides. Its carrier therefore records the environment anchor, the established state, and the scope within which that state remains reusable. These carrier types are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. task may therefore involve multiple carriers, and the same carrier may be revised as its underlying progress evolves. Execution Context. Execution context complements continuation carriers by retaining information needed for execution but not encoded in reusable task objects. It records the current focus, unresolved constraints and obligations, and pending work not materialized into reusable carrier. Live Tail. Live tail contains the original agentenvironment interactions accumulated since the most recent fold. These interactions remain directly available until incorporated into subsequent fold. At interaction step t, let denote the most recent fold and bk the last interaction step covered by that fold. The fold establishes maintained set of continuation carrier records Ak and execution context Ek, while interactions occurring afterward remain in the live tail Lt = (hbk+1, . . . , ht). The context view is therefore Vt = (Ak, Ek, Lt). (1) Here, Ak exposes reusable task progress, Ek preserves complementary information needed for continuation, and Lt retains interactions not yet folded. This view provides the basis for continuation: as execution proceeds, new interactions accumulate in the live tail, while subsequent folds update the maintained carriers and execution context without reconstructing previously established progress from scratch.

sections.title: 3.3 CONSTRUCTING AND UPDATING THE CONTEXT VIEW
sections.content: To maintain this context view during execution, CarryOn periodically folds accumulated interactions in the live tail into the maintained representation. Each fold identifies reusable progress, associates 4 it with supporting evidence, and preserves the information still needed for continuation. The update proceeds in four stages: tracking candidates, preparing evidence, joint compilation, and validation and commitment. Tracking Candidates. CarryOn first identifies progress that may become reusable in subsequent execution. The Tracker maintains candidates, each representing potential new carrier or an update to an existing one. As execution proceeds, candidates may remain under development across multiple Tracker invocations; once candidate has reached state that can support continuation, the Tracker requests its compilation. compilation request specifies both what should be compiled and the evidence needed to support it. For external objects and situated state, this includes the relevant environment object together with the state or conditions required for its reuse. For information products, it includes the source material from which reusable information should be retained. Candidates that are not yet ready remain tracked for later folds. Preparing Evidence. Before compilation, CarryOn first gathers the evidence authorized for each selected candidate. When compilation updates an existing carrier, it also includes the carriers current record. For information products, CarryOn checks that the selected material is consistent with its recorded sources. For external objects and situated state, it binds the request to the corresponding environment object, and the Grounder performs read-only checks of relevant conditions where available. The resulting input package Ut contains the selected candidates, applicable carrier records, authorized source material, object references, and available check results. This package fixes the record versions and evidence against which proposed carrier edits are later validated. Additional details are given in Appendix A.2. Joint Compilation. CarryOn jointly updates continuation carriers and execution context to preserve the information needed for subsequent execution. These updates are coupled: progress captured by carriers need not be duplicated in execution context, while unresolved goals, constraints, and unfinished work must remain explicit after fold. The Compiler receives the prepared input package Ut, containing the selected candidates, relevant prior carrier records and supporting evidence, together with the current execution context Ek and chronological text projection Π(Lt) of the live tail. It proposes carrier edits At and revised execution context (cid:98)Ek+1: (At, (cid:98)Ek+1) = Compile(Ut, Ek, Π(Lt)). (2) The Compiler proposes edits only for the selected candidates, grounding each edit in its authorized evidence. In contrast, the execution context is revised against the entire live tail to preserve continuation-relevant information. For external objects and situated state, the Compiler records reusable progress and its condition of use, while the underlying objects or states remain in the environment. For information products, it stores reusable findings directly in carrier records. In parallel, the Compiler revises execution context using the live tail, retaining active requirements and unfinished work not captured by carriers, including information outside the selected candidates. Upon successful validation, affected carriers receive successor versions, while unaffected carriers retain their existing records. Validation and Commitment. Before proposed update changes the active context, CarryOn checks that its carrier edits still refer to the current candidate and carrier versions and are consistent with the evidence authorized for their compilation requests. It also verifies the required identity, reference, and output constraints. successful fold must introduce at least one carrier change; revising the execution context alone does not retire interaction history. These checks guard the runtime against inconsistent or unsupported updates; they do not verify task correctness. If these checks fail, the existing context view and live tail remain unchanged. Otherwise, CarryOn atomically applies the carrier edits and commits the revised execution context, advancing the fold through the covered interactions. In the current implementation, successful fold covers the entire live tail. sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Benchmark. We evaluate CarryOn on OSWorld 2.0 (Yuan et al., 2026) and BrowseCompPlus (Chen et al., 2025) to assess its performance across different types of long-horizon tasks. We use the full OSWorld 2.0 benchmark as our primary evaluation for its long execution horizons, complex workflows, and task diversity. We additionally evaluate our method on randomly sampled subset of 100 BrowseComp-Plus questions, which require iterative search across multiple sources and provide complementary setting for studying context management over long search histories. Benchmark details are provided in Appendix B.1. Implementation. We use Claude Opus 4.7 for the host agent, CarryOns Tracker, and Compiler. We use 500-step budget per task on OSWorld 2.0, and the agent retrieves documents using BM25 (Robertson et al., 1995) on BrowseComp-Plus. Detailed experimental configurations and implementation settings are provided in Appendix A.3. Evaluation Metrics. On OSWorld 2.0, we report partial score and binary score, following the official evaluation protocol. On BrowseComp-Plus, we report answer accuracy, with final responses assessed by Qwen3-32B using the benchmarks official grading prompt. We measure efficiency through token usage per task and cost per task, including both agent and context-management calls. 6 Table 3: Task performance on the 100-question subset of BrowseComp-Plus. CarryOn improves the accuracy over the same Claude Opus 4.7 by 7%.

sections.title: 4.2 MAIN RESULT
sections.content: As shown in Table 1, CarryOn boosts the partial score from 43.9% to 49.7% and binary score from 15.7% to 19.4%, exceeding other frontier models. At the same time, CarryOn reduces total token usage by 51.9% and cost per task by 35.9% as demonstrated in Table 2. These results show that CarryOn reduces long-horizon execution cost without sacrificing task performance. We further evaluate CarryOn on random 100-question subset of BrowseComp-Plus. CarryOn raises accuracy from 49.0% to 56.0% over the Claude Opus 4.7 baseline, while the score is also above other frontier models shown in Table 3. At the same time, total token usage decreases by 22.9% and total cost by 7.1%. Together with the OSWorld results, this shows consistent pattern across computer-use and information-seeking tasks: CarryOn reduces context-processing overhead while maintaining or improving observed task performance.

As shown in Figure 3(a), the baseline context grows steadily with trajectory length, eventually exceeding 200K tokens, whereas CarryOns mean input context stabilizes at approximately 65K tokens after the initial growth phase. This indicates that our method maintains consistently compact context for the agent, regardless of how long execution continues. 7 Table 4: Comparison of different methods on shared 40-task subset of OSWorld 2.0. sections.title: 4.4 COMPARISON WITH CONTEXT MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES
sections.content: We examine the proposed object-oriented organization against conventional history compression, and compare the full CarryOn runtime with summary-based implementation of the same principles. On the same random 40-task subset of OSWorld 2.0, we compare: (i) Baseline, the default OSWorld 2.0 agent setting without additional context compression; (ii) Sliding Window, which retains only recent messages; (iii) Generic Summary (GS), which summarizes earlier history into continuation note; and (iv) CarryOn-Guided Summary (CGS), which applies our object-oriented organizing principles within textual summary. Sliding Window and GS follow the FIFO truncation and prompting-based summarization baselines of Kang et al. (2026). All methods use the same host model (Claude Opus 4.7), the same trigger condition, and the same step budget. As shown in Table 4, aggressive history compression does not improve performance by itself: Sliding Window and GS retain the shortest contexts but reduce both binary and partial scores relative to the baseline. Applying the same organizing principles through CGS recovers much of this loss, reaching 50.93% partial score. Full CarryOn further increases the partial score to 55.93% while matching the baseline binary score of 22.50%. Compared with CGS, CarryOn achieves 5.00% higher partial score with about 10% shorter post-fold text. Together, these results show that our object-oriented organization principle is effective even when applied within textual summary, while the full CarryOn runtime yields further improvements, demonstrating the additional benefit of maintaining and managing this structured state explicitly during execution.

sections.title: 4.5 ANALYSIS
sections.content: Carriers and the execution context are complementary. We conduct an ablation study on the shared 40-task OSWorld 2.0 subset by hiding either continuation carriers or execution context from the host agent. As shown in Table 5, removing execution context reduces binary score from 22.50% to 17.50% and partial score from 55.93% to 44.00%, while the number of agent calls changes little. The carriers still expose completed progress, but the agent loses complementary goals, constraints, and unresolved requirements needed to finish the task. Removing continuation carriers reduces partial score to 44.62%, while increasing agent calls by 23.8% and cost by 22.3%. Without direct access to established progress, the agent must recover or reproduce earlier results before continuing. This behavior is visible in trajectory-level examples in Appendix C.2. Together, the two ablations show that carriers and execution context preserve distinct, complementary information for continuation. Continuation carriers preserve and update progress across folds. To examine how carrier records evolve as execution progresses, we compare them before and after each committed fold in CarryOns OSWorld 2.0 trajectories. Figure 4(a) shows that 80% of carrier records are retained or updated. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce CarryOn, context runtime that organizes long-horizon agent context around reusable task objects. Our method combines continuation carriers that expose reusable progress, execution context that preserves complementary goals, constraints, and unresolved issues, and live tail of recent interactions. As the task progresses, CarryOn jointly updates continuation carriers and execution context to reflect evolving task state and remaining requirements, progressively replacing covered interaction history with an updated context view. On OSWorld 2.0, CarryOn raises partial score from 43.9% to 49.7% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and nominal model cost by 35.9%, including runtime overhead. On BrowseComp-Plus, it increases accuracy from 49% to 56% with lower token usage and cost. Together, these results support object-oriented context management for long-horizon agents, where task objects carry established progress and explicit context evolves with what is still needed to move forward.

sections.title: A METHOD AND IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 CONTEXT REPRESENTATION AND UPDATE PROCEDURE CarryOn maintains an append-only interaction log, candidate registry, versioned carrier records, and execution-context revisions. The committed carrier records and execution context define the folded portion of the context view; subsequent interactions form the live tail. Candidate Records. Each candidate has runtime-assigned identifier, provisional carrier type, short description, and references to the interactions supporting it. Its identity fields specify the associated object or subject, and it may refer to an existing carrier whose progress is being updated. The registry records when the candidate was first observed and last revised. Candidates can persist across Tracker invocations, allowing progress to accumulate before compilation. Registering or revising candidate does not itself trigger fold. Carrier Records and Versions. committed carrier record contains its identity, carrier type, reusable content or object reference, conditions for continuation, applicability scope, provenance, and version information. External-object identities are derived from their normalized locations. Information-product identities combine representation type with structured subject, while situated-state identities combine state domain with the subject of an environment anchor. These identity fields distinguish the object being tracked from its changing contents. Updating an existing carrier creates successor record linked to the previous version. The successor becomes current, while earlier versions remain stored for provenance. Carriers not changed by fold retain their current records. For information products, reusable content is stored as claims with identifiers, propositions, optional values, and supporting source references. Revisions can add, modify, or retract claims while carrying forward unaffected claims. Execution Context. Execution context is stored as revision associated with committed fold. It contains the current focus, continuity information needed to resume work, open obligations, active constraints, and immediate continuation instructions. Entries retain source attribution. The Compiler revises this information against the proposed carrier updates, preserving unresolved requirements and removing items that have been resolved or are now represented by carriers. Update Procedure. At each invocation, the runtime performs the following operations: 1. The Tracker reads recent interactions and the candidate registry. The runtime applies admissible candidate updates and resolves any compilation requests to their candidate records. 2. For each admitted request, the runtime binds the candidate snapshot, authorized prior carrier records, and supporting sources. Applicable environment checks contribute additional evidence. The resulting package fixes the records and evidence used for compilation. If no request is admitted, the invocation ends without fold. 3. The Compiler proposes carrier additions or revisions together with new execution context. Its input also includes the current execution context and chronological text projection of the live tail, so continuation information outside the selected candidates can be retained. 4. The runtime checks identity and reference consistency, source authorization, output constraints, and whether the compilation input records remain current. valid proposal must contain an actual carrier change. Acceptance atomically commits the carrier updates and execution-context revision and advances the fold boundary through the entire live tail. Rejection leaves these committed components and the live tail unchanged. Previously accepted candidate updates remain available after rejected compilation proposal. The original interactions remain in the log after successful fold. Grounder rules and installation of the committed view are described in Appendices A.2 and A.3, respectively. A.2 GROUNDER CHECKS AND VERDICT RULES CarryOn aligns compilation requests with their supporting evidence. Information products undergo source-reference and excerpt checks. A.3 AGENT INTEGRATION AND CARRYON SETTINGS Agent integration. CarryOn runs alongside the agent through benchmark-specific adapter. The adapter records interactions, supplies their textual representations and exposed thinking summaries to the runtime, and installs committed carrier records and execution context before the next agent call. Within each benchmark, the baseline and CarryOn use the same agent model, environmentaction interface, and task budget. CarryOn additionally supplies the context-management interfaces and feedback described below. Model configuration. We use Claude Opus 4.7 for the agent, Tracker, and Compiler, without additional training. Table 7 lists their output limits and execution budgets. On OSWorld 2.0, the agent uses adaptive thinking at maximum effort; Tracker and Compiler requests contain no explicit thinking or effort override. On BrowseComp-Plus, the agent uses adaptive thinking with the providers default effort, the Tracker uses adaptive thinking at high effort, and the Compiler has thinking disabled. Both adapters expose the providers summarized thinking output to the runtime, marking it as agent-generated information rather than environment observations. Runtime triggering. On OSWorld 2.0, the Tracker is normally invoked when interaction text accumulated since the previous scan or fold exceeds an estimated 6,000 tokens. This estimate is the character count of the runtimes text projection divided by four and excludes the agents thinking summaries. These thresholds measure text volume, not predicted monetary savings. On BrowseComp-Plus, scan scheduling uses growth in the agents recorded prompt size, including cached input. The initial trigger requires 120,000 tokens of growth plus 1,024-token margin and newly ingested search results. Consecutive scans that produce no fold double the token thresholds, up to six doublings; successful fold resets this backoff. 14 Table 7: Agent and CarryOn settings. sections.content: B.1 BENCHMARK AND TASK SELECTION OSWorld 2.0. OSWorld 2.0 contains long-horizon tasks spanning seven professional domains and 21 subcategories (Yuan et al., 2026). Its workflows combine desktop applications and web services, requiring cross-source reasoning, state tracking, and coordinated operations on multiple task outputs. The benchmark reports median estimated human completion time of approximately 1.6 hours. The duration and diversity of these workflows make it suitable for evaluating context management over extended task execution. We use the v2026.08.08 release. Our main OSWorld 2.0 evaluation covers the full evaluation set, with both the baseline agent and CarryOn independently run by us.
